title: Women singers' styles shifting toward stage and ballads
summary: The interviewers ask whether she saw herself as different from Ethel Waters and Alberta Hunter; she says she kept her church sound and did not change style.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Did you make any distinction between -- see, let's go back to when you first started to record. It was Ma Rainey and Bessie Smith and some --
Ida Cox (PHONETIC).
Ida Cox, Trixie Smith (PHONETIC), Clara (PHONTETIC).
Yeah.
Those girls there, they were older than you, for the most part. I think every one that we mentioned --
Well, I wouldn't have thought of Trixie and Clara --
Right, now, as the '20s went by, as it got older, and towards -- in the era, in the time when you were making records with Louie Armstrong, '26 and '27.
That was 1924 when Louie was with Fletcher Henderson in New York, right?
Uh-huh.

Well, her sessions with Louie were '25 and '26. But anyway, a couple years after you started to record, a few years after, something like that, there was a slight change in the type of music that the girls, the singers like yourself, were recording. Some of them were still singing the gut bucket blues and some of them were singing a little rag and a lot of them were singing more refined type of blues.
Yeah, (unintelligible).
Now, the question I have to ask is, like Ethel Waters, as an example. Ethel Waters began moving
away from the blues song and began getting --
She never did sing the blues.
-- into the ballads and then she went into even making movies.
Yeah, yes.

Right? And the same thing is true with Alberta Hunter, who was a blues singer like yourself and then began to sing jazz a little bit, okay? And more and more jazzy up-tempo type music, more updated in every respect. Musically it was more sophisticated, more --
More stage kind of music.
More stage, exactly.
More stage, more popular type.
Now, my question is this. You came from more of a country feeling. You had more of a Texas feeling, you had more --
Gospel.
Even Gospel, that's true.
Yeah.

You had more gospel feeling. Did you ever make a distinction between the type of songs and your type of singing and other singers that you knew? Did you ever feel that you were any different than any of them? Never?
When you saw Alberta last month on the TV, did you remember back in the '20s when you saw Alberta?
Did you ever see her at the Dreamland Cafe when you were in Chicago? No? You didn't see her in Chicago?
(Unintelligible).
Oh, you didn't go there. You didn't know Alberta in the '20s? Oh, you never knew her.
I knew her name, but I didn't know her.
I see.
I was kind of young. (Unintelligible), you know, I didn't know.
You didn't go around like that, uh-huh. Did it -- did you ever think about changing your style because those other women were changing their styles like Ethel Waters?
No, (inaudible).
You stayed with the church sound.
Uh-huh.
Uh-huh.
(Recording interruption.)
